newsitem.title: USA: Congressional Democrats split on budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Congressional Democrats split on budget deal.

text.p: House Democratic leaders howled betrayal, but Senate Democrats generally praised President Clinton on Thursday as the outline of a possible balanced budget deal with Republicans emerged.
Complaining they had been shut out of secret budget talks, liberal House Democrats lashed out at the White House.
They claimed the tentative pact betrayed party principles by dishing out tax cuts for the wealthy while stinting on programmes for the working class.

Saying he and other lawmakers had written to Clinton to express concerns, Massachusetts Representative Barney Frank sniped: "We addressed it to the Democratic president of the United States and it came back 'addressee unknown.'"

House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt groused that his troops had been locked out of the process. He said top Democratic budget writers showed up for what was supposed to be a key meeting on Wednesday, but no Republicans arrived.
"It's unfortunate this has not been a budget summit arrangement that has included House Democrats and probably Senate Democrats to the extent I would have liked," he said.

Gephardt is at odds with the White House on a host of issues, including trade. There is speculation he wants to challenge Vice President Al Gore for the presidency in 2000, a factor that has contributed to a tense relationship.
But conservative "Blue Dog" Democrats, an important swing bloc who had been avidly courted by Clinton, said they supported the agreement and predicted up to half the House Democrats might support it.
Twenty members of the group held a news conference to praise the emerging deal. "We're cheerleaders for the negotiating team," California Democrat Gary Condit said.
Across the Capitol, Senate Democrats were also more upbeat as they emerged from an afternoon briefing with White House budget chief Franklin Raines.
"Overall this is an extraordinary accomplishment, really a historic accomplishment," Connecticut Democratic Sen. Joe Lieberman said.
Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle complained on Thursday morning that "the process stinks." But he was more sanguine after the afternoon briefing.

"I don't want to sound too euphoric here until we've been able to see just what the results of negotiations are, but the framework that was explained to us is certainly satisfactory," he said, adding half his colleagues might back it.

Senate Democrats, who hold 45 seats in the 100-member chamber, know they will have far more influence as a deal moves through Congress than their House counterparts due to procedural rules that give the minority greater power.
They have also shown on past issues, such as welfare, that they are more willing to move toward the centre.

The White House and Republican leaders were still trying to work out final details of the budget plan. It was expected to include $115 billion in Medicare cuts over five years, a cap on spending in the Medicaid health programme for the poor and about $135 billion in gross tax cuts.
The tax cuts are higher than Democrats had wanted and include a capital gains cut that in past years most opposed.

The plan avoids major cost increases for Medicare beneficiaries. But Democrats, who attacked Republicans on the issue in the 1996 elections, have been worried they will lose their edge on the potent issue if they agree to deep cuts.
